title: Week 116 · Lesson 140: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment, Function & Frailty — FNP-Level Older-Adult Safety
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 116 — Lesson 140: Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment, Function & Frailty

FNP-level goal: Evaluate the older adult through function, mobility, cognition, mood, medications, nutrition, sensory health, continence, social support, safety, and goals—not disease count alone—and recognize acute decline, delirium, falls, medication harm, mistreatment, and caregiver failure before they become crises.

Learning Objectives

  • Organize a comprehensive geriatric assessment around medical, functional, cognitive, psychological, social, environmental, and goal-based domains.
  • Measure activities of daily living, instrumental activities, mobility, fall risk, and frailty while identifying reversible contributors.
  • Differentiate delirium, dementia, and depression and treat sudden cognitive change as an acute medical problem.
  • Conduct medication reconciliation and deprescribing using indication, benefit horizon, burden, interaction, renal function, and patient priorities.
  • Assess caregiver capacity, driving, home safety, nutrition, continence, sensory loss, capacity, and advance-care planning.

Part 1 — Aging Is Heterogeneous

Chronologic age does not define health. Two people of the same age may have completely different reserve, function, cognition, and goals. Avoid attributing fatigue, falls, incontinence, confusion, weight loss, or pain to “just getting older.” Each may reflect treatable disease, medication harm, environmental mismatch, or unmet support.

The FNP asks not only “What diagnoses are present?” but also “What can this person do, what changed, what matters most, and what threatens independence or safety?”

Part 2 — What Is Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment?

CGA is a structured, multidimensional process that identifies medical conditions, function, cognition, mood, mobility, nutrition, medication, sensory impairment, continence, social resources, environment, caregiver needs, and personal goals. It produces a coordinated plan with named ownership rather than a longer problem list.

The assessment can be staged across visits when the patient is stable. An acute decline, however, should not be delayed for a future wellness appointment.

Part 3 — Begin With What Matters

Ask what activities make life meaningful, what the patient wants to preserve, which symptoms are most disruptive, and which treatments feel burdensome. A plan focused only on disease targets can worsen dizziness, falls, fatigue, cost, or treatment workload without improving the person's priorities.

Use supported communication: hearing devices, glasses, interpreter, plain language, adequate time, and direct conversation with the patient. A caregiver is an important collateral source but should not automatically replace the patient's voice.

Part 4 — Function: ADLs and IADLs

Basic activities of daily living include bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, and eating. Instrumental activities include medication management, finances, transportation, shopping, cooking, housekeeping, communication, and appointment coordination. Ask what the patient actually does—not merely what they say they “could” do.

A new IADL problem may be the earliest sign of cognitive decline, vision loss, depression, medication effect, or neurologic disease. New ADL dependence often signals greater severity and may determine whether home remains safe.

Part 5 — Mobility and Performance

Observe rising from a chair, standing balance, gait initiation, stride, turning, assistive-device use, footwear, and endurance. Validated tools such as gait speed, chair stand, and Timed Up and Go can help quantify change when used correctly. Examine strength, joints, feet, sensation, orthostatic blood pressure, vision, and neurologic function.

Do not describe a patient as “noncompliant” for not using a walker before checking fit, training, home layout, stigma, cognition, and whether the device is within reach.

Part 6 — Falls Are a Syndrome

Ask about falls in the past year, near falls, injury, circumstances, loss of consciousness, dizziness, footwear, toileting urgency, nighttime lighting, alcohol, and fear of falling. Review gait, balance, lower-extremity strength, postural blood pressure, vision, feet, medication, cognition, cardiovascular symptoms, and environment.

CDC STEADI organizes care as screen, assess, and intervene. USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for community-dwelling adults 65 and older at increased fall risk and individualized multifactorial intervention. Effective plans may include balance and strength training, physical or occupational therapy, medication changes, vision care, home modification, continence management, and treatment of contributing disease.

Part 7 — A Fall May Be Syncope

Clarify whether the patient tripped, lost consciousness, had palpitations, chest pain, focal weakness, seizure features, or postevent confusion. Unwitnessed “falls” can reflect arrhythmia, orthostasis, stroke, seizure, hypoglycemia, bleeding, or infection. Head injury risk is greater with anticoagulation.

Emergency evaluation is required for new neurologic deficit, persistent altered status, suspected significant head injury, inability to bear weight, major bleeding, chest pain, hemodynamic instability, or high-risk syncope.

Part 8 — Frailty and Sarcopenia

Frailty is reduced physiologic reserve and vulnerability to stressors. Clues include slowed gait, weakness, exhaustion, reduced activity, and unintentional weight loss. Sarcopenia emphasizes loss of muscle strength and mass. Neither is an inevitable label that ends treatment; both identify higher risk from illness, surgery, medication, and hospitalization.

Assess reversible contributors such as inadequate protein or calories, dental disease, depression, endocrine disease, inflammation, medication, inactivity, pain, and social isolation. Management commonly combines progressive resistance and balance activity, nutrition support, disease treatment, and realistic functional goals.

Part 9 — Cognition: Establish the Time Course

Ask the patient and a knowledgeable informant about memory, language, navigation, medication, finances, cooking, safety events, and change from baseline. Use a validated cognitive instrument when concern exists, followed by diagnostic assessment rather than treating a screen score as a diagnosis.

Consider hearing, language, education, culture, sleep, depression, substances, medication, metabolic disease, and neurologic illness. Cognitive impairment does not automatically eliminate decision-making capacity; capacity is specific to a decision and time.

Part 10 — Delirium Is Acute Brain Failure

Delirium develops over hours to days, fluctuates, and involves impaired attention or awareness. It may be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed; a quiet sleepy patient can be missed. Dementia usually develops progressively over months to years, although delirium commonly occurs on top of dementia.

Search urgently for infection, medication toxicity or withdrawal, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, electrolyte or glucose abnormality, organ failure, stroke, seizure, trauma, and environmental disruption. Treat the cause and use orientation, mobility, sleep support, sensory aids, hydration, and family presence. Sedating medication can worsen outcomes and is not routine treatment for confusion.

Part 11 — Depression, Grief, and Isolation

Depression may present as low mood, anhedonia, sleep or appetite change, slowed thinking, pain, fatigue, or cognitive complaint. Screen with a validated tool and assess suicide risk. Grief and loneliness are not automatically disorders but can coexist with depression and medical decline.

Ask about social contact, bereavement, transportation, purpose, community, and technology access. NIA notes that isolation and loneliness are associated with depression, cardiovascular disease, and cognitive decline. Connect patients to meaningful activities and services that they accept.

Part 12 — Medication Reconciliation and Deprescribing

Ask the patient to bring prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, sleep aids, antihistamines, supplements, cannabis, and alcohol history. For each item, ask: Is there a current indication? Is it effective? Is the dose appropriate for kidney and liver function? Does it duplicate another drug? Can it cause falls, bleeding, confusion, constipation, retention, hypotension, or hypoglycemia? Can the patient obtain and manage it?

The AGS Beers Criteria identifies potentially inappropriate medications, not drugs that must be stopped automatically. Consider goals, alternatives, palliative context, withdrawal risk, and shared decision-making. Taper agents that cause physiologic dependence. Simplify schedules and assign a medication owner after hospitalization.

Part 13 — Nutrition, Oral Health, and Swallowing

Unintentional weight loss is a clinical signal. Assess food access, appetite, taste and smell, dentition, dry mouth, swallowing, mood, cognition, medication, malignancy, gastrointestinal disease, and ability to shop or cook. Observe whether meals require setup or feeding help.

Coughing with meals, wet voice, recurrent pneumonia, prolonged eating, or unexplained weight loss raises concern for dysphagia and aspiration. Coordinate speech-language evaluation and nutrition support rather than simply prescribing appetite stimulants.

Part 14 — Vision, Hearing, and Continence

Sensory loss can mimic cognitive decline, worsen falls, and increase isolation. Ask about hearing aids, cerumen, glasses, vision change, and ability to use devices. Sudden vision or hearing loss requires urgent evaluation.

Incontinence is not normal aging. Classify urge, stress, overflow, functional, or mixed patterns and look for infection, retention, constipation, mobility barriers, diuretics, delirium, and environmental access. New retention with pain, kidney injury, fever, or neurologic deficit is urgent.

Part 15 — Home, Driving, and Community Safety

Ask about stairs, lighting, grab bars, rugs, bathroom access, heating and cooling, food, emergency response, firearms, scams, and transportation. Occupational therapy home assessment can reveal hazards missed in clinic. Driving assessment should include crashes, near misses, getting lost, vision, cognition, motor function, medication, and collateral observations.

A diagnosis alone does not decide driving ability. Follow state reporting law and use objective evaluation or driving rehabilitation resources when uncertainty remains.

Part 16 — Caregiver Assessment

Identify who provides care, what tasks they perform, whether they understand the plan, and whether they have physical, emotional, financial, and respite capacity. Caregiver burnout can present as missed medication, conflict, delayed care, or inability to maintain hygiene and nutrition.

Offer home health, therapy, adult day services, respite, social work, transportation, meal support, and Eldercare resources when eligible. Supporting the caregiver protects the patient, but the caregiver's preference does not automatically override a capable patient's choice.

Part 17 — Elder Mistreatment

Interview the patient privately when possible. Ask about physical harm, threats, unwanted sexual contact, neglect, financial exploitation, medication withholding, isolation, and fear. Clues include unexplained injuries, poor hygiene, malnutrition, repeated missed care, controlling companions, or financial changes.

Address immediate safety, document objectively, treat injuries, involve social work or adult protective services, and follow mandatory-reporting law. Avoid confronting a suspected perpetrator in a way that increases danger.

Part 18 — Capacity and Advance-Care Planning

Capacity requires understanding relevant information, appreciating consequences, reasoning about options, and communicating a choice. It is decision-specific and can fluctuate. Dementia does not automatically mean incapacity, and an unwise choice does not alone prove incapacity.

Discuss surrogate decision makers, advance directives, goals, hospitalization preferences, and what outcomes would be unacceptable before a crisis. Revisit after major health changes. Advance-care planning supports autonomy; it is not a one-time form or a signal that treatment is being abandoned.

Part 19 — Prioritize Multimorbidity

Multiple disease-specific guidelines can produce conflicting targets, polypharmacy, cost, and treatment burden. Prioritize conditions by immediate harm, symptom impact, functional benefit, time to benefit, and patient goals. Prevention remains important, but screening and treatment should be individualized to health status, life expectancy, willingness, and ability to benefit.

Write one integrated plan that says what changes now, what is monitored, which goals are relaxed, and who follows each issue.

Clinical Case 1 — “More Forgetful” for Two Days

An 82-year-old with mild dementia becomes sleepy, inattentive, and unable to manage meals over 48 hours after a medication change. The FNP treats this as possible hypoactive delirium, evaluates medication toxicity and acute medical causes urgently, and does not label it inevitable dementia progression.

Clinical Case 2 — The Fall Was Not Mechanical

A 76-year-old reports “tripping” twice but later describes sudden palpitations and brief loss of awareness. Orthostatic measurement, ECG and cardiac risk assessment, medication review, and urgent disposition replace a home-rug recommendation alone.

Clinical Case 3 — Twelve Medications and One Goal

An 88-year-old with dizziness, recurrent falls, hypoglycemia, and complex dosing says staying safely at home matters most. The FNP reconciles every drug, reduces fall- and hypoglycemia-promoting burden through shared deprescribing, arranges strength and balance support, and confirms follow-up ownership.

FNP High-Yield Framework: GERIATRIC

  1. G — Goals first: what matters, acceptable burden, meaningful function.
  2. E — Evaluate function: ADLs, IADLs, gait, falls, frailty, driving.
  3. R — Review cognition and mood: time course, delirium, dementia, depression, capacity.
  4. I — Inventory medications: indication, interaction, renal dose, adverse effects, deprescribing.
  5. A — Assess nutrition and senses: weight, oral health, swallowing, vision, hearing, continence.
  6. T — Test the support system: home, caregiver capacity, finances, transportation, mistreatment.
  7. R — Respond to acute change: confusion, fall injury, syncope, neurologic deficit, retention, dehydration.
  8. I — Individualize prevention: benefit horizon, function, preferences, access.
  9. C — Close every transition: medication owner, referrals, community services, advance plan.

Take-Home Summary

Geriatric primary care is organized around reserve, function, safety, and goals. Falls are multifactorial, frailty may be modifiable, sudden confusion is delirium until evaluated, and medication benefit must be balanced against real-world burden. The care plan succeeds only when the patient and support system can carry it out.

Educational note: Follow current CDC STEADI, USPSTF, AGS medication, local capacity, driving, mistreatment-reporting, and emergency guidance. Acute confusion, focal neurologic change, high-risk syncope, major fall injury, shock, severe medication toxicity, unsafe neglect, or inability to maintain essential care requires urgent evaluation.
